text: The Minute Man is an 1874 sculpture by Daniel Chester French located in Minute Man National Historical Park in Concord, Massachusetts. Created between 1871 and 1874 after extensive research, it was originally intended to be made of stone but was switched to bronze and cast from ten Civil War-era cannons appropriated by Congress. The statue depicts a minuteman stepping away from his plow to join the patriot forces at the Battle of Concord, the start of the American Revolutionary War, with an overcoat thrown over the plow and a musket in hand. Nineteenth-century art historians noted the pose resembled the Apollo Belvedere, leading to the assumption it was copied from that statue; however, based on French's journals, modern art historians have shown that the Apollo Belvedere was only one of several classical statues used in the research. The statue was unveiled on April 19, 1875, during the centennial of the Battle of Concord, in a ceremony attended by President Ulysses S. Grant and Ralph Waldo Emerson, though French, who left for Italy in 1874, was not present—his absence was reportedly to avoid criticism. The statue received critical acclaim and continues to be praised by art historians and commentators. Minutemen, or Minute Companies, were a militia force in the Province of Massachusetts Bay, formed in response to the Powder Alarm in September 1774, and consisted of young volunteers paid one shilling, eight pence for drilling three times a week; unlike the general militia, their officers were elected by peers. By February 1775, Concord had 104 minutemen in two companies. In 1775, the Massachusetts Provincial Congress designated Concord as the stockpile for patriot cannons, gunpowder, and ammunition. British General Thomas Gage, acting on reports from spies and instructions from William Legge, Earl of Dartmouth, ordered a preemptive strike. On April 19, 1775, British troops under Major John Pitcairn met 70 militiamen under John Parker on Lexington Common, with Paul Revere, William Dawes, and Samuel Prescott alerting them; after less than 30 minutes of fighting, eight militiamen were killed and nine wounded. The British then moved to Concord, where 150 minutemen from Concord and Lincoln mustered on the Concord Common under James Barrett. After meeting the British, they retreated to higher ground without firing a shot. The British searched the town, destroying cannons, musket balls, and flour, though gunpowder was removed. The minutemen moved to the Old North Bridge and were reinforced, where 400 militiamen and minutemen repelled the British and forced them to retreat. Many returned home afterward, though skirmishes continued during the British retreat. In 1825, the Bunker Hill Monument Association donated $500 (equivalent to $13,900 in 2024) to build a monument to the Battle of Concord, originally planned near the town pump, but due to town disagreements, the funds were not used until Ezra Ripley donated land near the Old North Bridge in 1835. Solomon Willard designed a 25-foot-tall (7.6-meter) granite obelisk to commemorate the 60th anniversary, with Ralph Waldo Emerson writing "The Concord Hymn" for its dedication in 1836, sung to the tune of "Old Hundred." The obelisk stood on the riverbank where the British had fought, which displeased Emerson, who preferred it be placed where the militia stood. The Minute Man was created for the centennial and placed on the bank where the militia stood. The monument committee, including George M. Brooks, John B. More, John S. Keyes, and Emerson, selected Daniel Chester French because he was from Concord and his father, Henry F. French, was a prominent local lawyer and former judge. French's first full-size work, it was commissioned in 1889, with French having begun work on it in 1871. He sketched various poses and created a small clay figure rejected by the committee; a second clay model was accepted in 1873. The medium was changed to bronze that same year. A miniature version won a local art competition in September 1873 but was criticized for being "awkwardly stiff." The pose was refined through working with models, and by September 1874, the statue was completed. A plaster version was sent to Ames Manufacturing Works in Chicopee, Massachusetts. The town lacked funds to cast it in bronze, so through a bill introduced by Ebenezer R. Hoar, Congress appropriated ten Civil War-era cannons to the project. The statue is 7 feet (2.1 meters) tall and is possibly a portrait of Isaac Davis, an officer who died in the battle. The farmer-turned-soldier is shown trading his plow for a musket and stepping away from his private life, with sleeves rolled up and the overcoat draped over the plow; a powder horn mistakenly sits on his back. His face is alert, eyes fixed on the battle, and he wears a wide-brimmed hat pinned on the right side. The pose has been compared to the Apollo Belvedere, with critics like Lorado Taft and H. C. Howard suggesting it was directly copied, though modern scholarship, using French's journals, shows the pose was inspired by multiple classical sculptures, not a direct copy. The statue was intended to be placed on a local boulder, but at the insistence of French and his father, a stone pedestal was designed. Several architects submitted designs, including French's brother, with James Elliot Cabot winning the competition. The resulting pedestal is 7.5 feet (2.3 meters) tall and 4.5 feet (1.4 meters) wide, with inscriptions: the first stanza of "Concord Hymn" on the front and the battle date and centennial year on the rear. Beneath the pedestal is a copper time capsule from 1875 containing items from past celebrations, maps, and photographs, and a second capsule placed in 1975 with Girl Scouts USA pins, the United States Bicentennial flag, and a cassette tape. The statue is highly regarded by art historians and critics, with Rudyard Kipling nearly choking upon seeing it in 1892, Anna Seaton-Schmidt calling it "the most inspiring of our soldier monuments," the Boston National Historic Sites Commission stating it "perfectly personifies the American Patriot," Michael Richman calling it a "masterwork in nineteenth-century American sculpture," Chris Bergeron describing it as "naturalistic detail imbued with an idealistic effect," and Harold Holzer noting its "naturalism, a great feeling of humanity, and connection to the subject." Louisa May Alcott criticized the lack of women's presence at the unveiling, and suffragettes later adopted the statue as a symbol of their struggle for voting rights, making pilgrimages to it in the 1880s. The Minute Man is widely used by the U.S. government to represent the citizen-soldier, commemorate the Battle of Concord, and symbolize Massachusetts. It appears on the seal of the United States National Guard and its components, the Army National Guard and the Air National Guard. In 1925, the U.S. Post Office Department released a five-cent stamp featuring the statue and verses from "Concord Hymn." The U.S. Treasury has used it on war bonds and savings bonds, and workplaces and schools with a 90% war bond participation rate were authorized to fly a flag with the statue during World War II. The statue has appeared on U.S. coins twice: on the obverse of the 1925 Lexington–Concord Sesquicentennial half dollar and on the reverse of the 2000 Massachusetts state quarter, which also includes an outline of the state.
